 Emily Byrd Mon, November 9, 2026 at 2:53 PM UTC 2 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. Is the Triad in for an icy winter? FOX8 Meteorologist Emily Byrd shares 2026-27 winter weather prediction PIEDMONT TRIAD, N.C. (WGHP) — In the midst of a Super El Niño, this is going to be a tough winter to predict in the Carolinas. The current Super El Niño is forecast to last through February, so its influence on our winter weather predictions is substantial.
 El Niño winters are typically wetter than normal but also slightly warmer than normal in North Carolina.  There is no reason to expect any difference in this type of pattern for the upcoming winter, but that doesn't mean we're not expecting frozen precipitation. As any North Carolinian knows, we have a unique weather pattern that makes winter forecasting difficult:  The Appalachian Wedge.
  Will the Triad see snow? FOX8 Chief Meteorologist Van Denton shares 2026-27 winter weather prediction  
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement The Appalachian Wedge is a cool pool of air that develops across the Piedmont, west of the mountains. It develops when a steady, northeast wind brings Arctic air down the lee side of the Appalachian chain from New England. If the cold air mass is shallow, any moisture falling through it may be freezing rain or sleet. If the air mass is deep enough, it can produce snow.  The forecast gets difficult when the cold air is varying in depth from the Foothills to the Triad, and that's when we deal with snow totals on one side of the viewing area, and ice or cold rain a few counties away.  
 An El Niño season brings a southern jet stream into the Pacific southwest that streaks flatly across the country, along the Gulf Coast. This pattern tends to inhibit big surges of cold air from plunging southward, down the East Coast, and instead keeps the southern half of the country wetter than normal.  
 Taking this all into account, my winter weather prediction is for a wetter, slightly warmer winter.  There will still be a few cold snaps, but the cold air may not be deep enough to support widespread or deep snowfall. It's more likely we will have icy weather with perhaps one accumulation of snow in the Piedmont of less than 3 inches. Timing for wintry precipitation is most favorable for late January, just after our climatological coldest time of year.  
 Here are Emily's predictions:
 Colder or warmer? Warmer-than-normal temperatures with a few cold spells
 Advertisement Advertisement Coldest temperature? 18 degrees
 Largest snowfall? 2 inches with a higher chance of ice
 How many inches of snow? 2.5 inches
 First snow? Jan. 31
